query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐temperature corrosive environments (such as liquid lead or lead–bismuth eutectic used in nuclear reactors and chemical-processing plants), steels resist corrosion by rapidly forming a dual‐protective oxide film. The inner layer is enriched in Al (and/or modified by Si) forming a continuous, dense Al2O3-rich barrier, while the outer layer is enriched in Cr (or contains a mixed Cr/Si oxide) that further limits oxygen ingress and metal dissolution. This two‐tiered oxide structure—its formation promoted by fine-grained microstructures and appropriate oxygen levels—significantly retards both dissolution of Fe from the matrix and oxygen diffusion into the steel.
generation.material_initial_state: Ferritic/martensitic steels or ODS steels formulated with basic Cr content and either with or without additional alloying elements (e.g., Al and/or Si) in their as-manufactured state.
generation.intervention: Expose otherwise identical steel specimens—with controlled variations in Al and/or Si content—to a high-temperature liquid metal (e.g., liquid Pb or LBE) environment at controlled oxygen concentrations.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (approximately 550–700 °C) in oxygen-controlled corrosive media (liquid Pb or lead–bismuth eutectic), typical of advanced nuclear or chemical-processing applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The in-situ formation of a dual-layer oxide scale consisting of a dense, continuous Al2O3-rich inner layer (possibly modified by Si) and a secondary Cr-enriched (or mixed Cr/Si) outer layer.
generation.mechanism: Due to the high oxygen affinity of Al (and the stabilizing influence of additional Si), the inner oxide layer forms rapidly and continuously. This layer serves as a barrier to outward diffusion of Fe and inward ingress of oxygen and corrosive species. The outer Cr-rich oxide (or mixed oxide) further reinforces the barrier by reducing surface dissolution. A fine-grained microstructure (as found in ODS steels) further accelerates the beneficial diffusion kinetics, ensuring a robust, adherent, and protective oxide film under sustained high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to steels lacking extra Al (or Si), those with optimized Al/Si additions will develop thinner, more uniform and adherent oxide films, resulting in significantly reduced corrosion depth (on the order of a ~40% reduction as observed in 9CrAl ODS versus 9Cr ODS steels) and improved long-term stability of the protective barrier.
generation.baseline: Steels of similar composition but without the enhanced Al/Si addition and with coarser oxide layers, exhibiting faster element dissolution and poorer overall corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in high-temperature, oxygen-regulated liquid metal environments (e.g., liquid Pb or LBE) typical of nuclear and chemical-processing applications. It may not apply in low-temperature aqueous or chloride-dominated environments where corrosion mechanisms and oxide-film behavior differ.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from studies on Al-containing ODS steels (PMC10054900, sections from introduction and conclusions) and Si-enhanced T91 steels (PMC9028533) to posit that a similar dual-oxide mechanism operates broadly in these harsh environments. While the evidence suggests benefits from both alloying elements and microstructural refinement, the exact interplay of oxide-film formation kinetics and long-term stability under reactor-relevant conditions requires further verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel specimens with identical base chemistry and microstructural conditions but differing only in the content of Al (and/or Si). Expose both sets to a controlled high-temperature liquid Pb or LBE environment at regulated oxygen potential for the same duration. Employ microstructural characterization methods (SEM, TEM, XRD) to analyze the oxide scale, and use profilometry or weight loss measurements to assess the corrosion depth.
measurements: Oxide film thickness, continuity, and phase composition (via TEM, EDS, and XRD)
Corrosion depth or weight loss measurements
Surface morphology and microstructural integrity after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If steels with enhanced Al (and/or Si) content do not form a denser, thinner, and more protective dual-layer oxide scale or if their measured corrosion rate and depth do not significantly improve (e.g., fail to show at least ~40% reduction relative to baseline specimens), then the hypothesis that resistance is governed by the formation of the dual protective oxide film would be falsified.

The main conclusions obtained are as follows: The surface color and luster of the different corrode materials were quite different. The color of T91 is abundant with a metallic luster due to the formation of complex oxidation products and attached lead. Most of the surface of 9Cr ODS is gray-white with a metallic luster due to the covered metallic lead. The color of the 9CrAl surface is quite uniform without metallic luster; The corrosion of 9Cr ODS is slightly heavier than that of T91 after corrosion for 1000 h. AbstractThe 9–12% Cr ferritic–martensitic heat-resistant steel is the main candidate structural material for the Lead-cooled Faster Reactor. The lower Gibbs free energy change of Si oxide can promote the formation of a stable oxide layer, which can improve the corrosion resistance of the material. Therefore, it is of great significance to study the effect of silicon (Si) on the corrosion resistance of T91 steel in lead–bismuth eutectic (LBE). The corrosion resistance of T91 steel with Si contents of 0.5 wt.%, 1.3 wt.%, and 2.0 wt.%, both in dynamic and static LBE at 550 °C, was investigated. The microstructure was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscope (SEM) and transmission electron microscope (TEM), while the oxide films were characterized by electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). Results show that the addition of Si is conducive to improving the corrosion resistance of T91 steel in LBE. T91 steel with high Si content has a thinner and more stable oxide film. The change of Si content can change the contact angle between the steel and LBE, and the contact angle is the largest when the Si content is 1.3 wt.%.
